```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggraph)
library(tidygraph)
library(kableExtra)

# ---- Guiding example: ego + 8 alters (a-h) on a circle ----------------------
alt_names <- letters[1:8]

make_pos <- function(alters) {
  n <- length(alters)
  ang <- pi/2 - (0:(n - 1)) * (2 * pi / n)
  data.frame(
    name = c("Ego", alters),
    x = c(0, cos(ang)),
    y = c(0, sin(ang))
  )
}

mk_pairs <- function(...) {
  p <- list(...)
  if (length(p) == 1 && !is.null(dim(p[[1]]))) {
    return(data.frame(from = p[[1]][, 1], to = p[[1]][, 2]))
  }
  p <- unlist(p)
  data.frame(from = substr(p, 1, 1), to = substr(p, 2, 2))
}

# Base network from the lecture deck: 10 alter-alter ties
base_pairs <- mk_pairs("ab", "ah", "ag", "bh", "bg", "de", "dg", "ef", "fg", "gh")

# Effective-size example 1 (dense alter-alter ties): 14 ties, ES = 4.5
dense_pairs <- mk_pairs("ab", "ag", "ah", "bc", "be", "bg", "bh",
                        "cd", "de", "dg", "ef", "eg", "fg", "gh")

# Effective-size example 2 (sparse alter-alter ties): 7 ties, ES = 6.25
sparse_pairs <- mk_pairs("ab", "ag", "ah", "bh", "gh", "de", "ef")

# Effective-size limits: no ties (max) and complete alter-alter graph (min), m = 28
complete_pairs <- mk_pairs(apply(combn(alt_names, 2), 2, paste, collapse = ""))

# Attribute figures (composition / homophily / diversity) use the pure star — no alter-alter ties, since those measures don't depend on them
kin_pairs     <- mk_pairs()
same_pairs    <- mk_pairs()
diverse_pairs <- mk_pairs()

# Clustering worked examples
clustered_pairs   <- mk_pairs("ab", "ac", "ad", "bc", "bd", "cd",       # K4 clique 1
                              "ef", "eg", "eh", "fg", "fh", "gh",       # K4 clique 2
                              "de", "bf", "cg", "ah", "be")             # 5 cross-circle ties, m = 17
mid_pairs         <- mk_pairs("ab", "ac", "bc", "fg", "fh", "gh", "df")  # 2 triangles + bridge, m = 7
unclustered_pairs <- mk_pairs("ab", "cd", "ef", "gh")                    # disjoint pairs, m = 4

# ---- Plot helper -------------------------------------------------------------
ego_plot <- function(pairs, alters = alt_names, labels = NULL, pal = NULL,
                     show_ego_ties = TRUE, node_legend = FALSE, ego_label = "Ego",
                     legend_nrow = NULL) {
  # labels: named vector name -> category; pal: named palette for categories
  pos <- make_pos(alters)
  edges <- rbind(
    data.frame(from = "Ego", to = alters, tie = "Ego-alter")
  )
  if (nrow(pairs) > 0) {
    edges <- rbind(edges, data.frame(from = pairs$from, to = pairs$to, tie = "Alter-alter"))
  }
  if (!show_ego_ties) edges <- edges[edges$tie == "Alter-alter", ]
  nd <- pos
  if (is.null(labels)) {
    nd$cat <- ifelse(nd$name == "Ego", ego_label, "Alter")
  } else {
    nd$cat <- ifelse(nd$name == "Ego", ego_label, unname(labels[nd$name]))
  }
  nd$cat[is.na(nd$cat) & nd$name != "Ego"] <- "Alter"
  if (is.null(pal)) pal <- c(setNames("steelblue", "Alter"), setNames("grey30", ego_label))
  g <- tbl_graph(nodes = nd, edges = edges, directed = FALSE)
  p <- ggraph(g, layout = "manual", x = nd$x, y = nd$y) +
    geom_edge_link(aes(color = tie, linetype = tie), width = 1.3) +
    scale_edge_color_manual(
      values = c("Ego-alter" = "grey75", "Alter-alter" = "darkorchid"),
      guide = "none"
    ) +
    scale_edge_linetype_manual(
      values = c("Ego-alter" = "solid", "Alter-alter" = "dashed"),
      guide = "none"
    ) +
    geom_node_point(aes(color = cat), size = 14) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = pal, name = NULL,
      breaks = setdiff(unique(nd$cat[nd$name != "Ego"]), NA),
      guide = if (node_legend) guide_legend(nrow = legend_nrow) else "none"
    ) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.45, 1.45), ylim = c(-1.45, 1.45), clip = "off") +
    theme_graph()
  if (node_legend) {
    p <- p + theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
      legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")
    )
  }
  p
}

# ---- Effective-size computation ---------------------------------------------
es_calc <- function(pairs, n_alter = 8) {
  m <- nrow(pairs)
  S <- n_alter
  avg_deg <- 2 * m / n_alter
  data.frame(m = m, n = n_alter, avg_deg = avg_deg, ES = S - avg_deg)
}

# ---- Adjacency matrix table --------------------------------------------------
adj_kable <- function(pairs, highlight_m = FALSE) {
  A <- matrix(0, length(alt_names), length(alt_names),
              dimnames = list(alt_names, alt_names))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(pairs))) {
    A[pairs$from[i], pairs$to[i]] <- 1
    A[pairs$to[i], pairs$from[i]] <- 1
  }
  if (highlight_m) {
    D <- A
    for (i in seq_along(alt_names)) {
      for (j in seq_along(alt_names)) {
        if (j > i && A[i, j] == 1) {
          D[i, j] <- cell_spec("1", background = "darkorchid",
                               color = "white", bold = TRUE)
        }
      }
    }
    knitr::kable(D, format = "html", escape = FALSE) |>
      kable_styling(font_size = 18, bootstrap_options = "condensed", full_width = FALSE) |>
      column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
  } else {
    knitr::kable(A, format = "html", escape = FALSE) |>
      kable_styling(font_size = 18, bootstrap_options = "condensed", full_width = FALSE) |>
      column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
  }
}

# ---- Attribute label vectors (real-demographic register, HW7 style) ---------
# Ego identifies as Black and as a Man.
race_labels   <- c(a = "White", b = "Black", c = "White", d = "Asian",
                   e = "Hispanic", f = "Black", g = "White", h = "Asian")
gender_labels <- c(a = "Man", b = "Man", c = "Woman", d = "Man",
                   e = "Nonbinary", f = "Man", g = "Man", h = "Woman")
kin_labels    <- c(a = "Kin", b = "Kin", c = "Non-kin", d = "Non-kin",
                   e = "Kin", f = "Kin", g = "Kin", h = "Non-kin")
race_pal   <- c(White = "steelblue", Black = "darkorange",
                Asian = "forestgreen", Hispanic = "purple")
gender_pal <- c(Man = "steelblue", Woman = "darkorange", Nonbinary = "forestgreen")

# Homophily (negative E-I) example: ego is Black, 6 Black alters, 2 White (c, g)
race_labels_h <- c(a = "Black", b = "Black", c = "White", d = "Black",
                   e = "Black", f = "Black", g = "White", h = "Black")

# Low-diversity example: ego is Black, 7 White alters, 1 Black (f)
race_labels_l <- c(a = "White", b = "White", c = "White", d = "White",
                   e = "White", f = "Black", g = "White", h = "White")

# ---- Blau index for the diversity example (White 3, Black 2, Asian 2, Hispanic 1)
blau <- function(counts) {
  p <- counts / sum(counts)
  H <- 1 - sum(p^2)
  Hmax <- 1 - 1 / length(counts)
  data.frame(H = H, Hmax = Hmax, ratio = H / Hmax)
}
```

## Ego Networks: The Basic Ingredients

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- **Ego**: the central node whose network we are describing.

. . .

- **Alters**: the nodes surrounding ego.

. . .

- **Ego-alter ties are obligatory**: every alter is connected to ego.

. . .

- **Alter-alter ties are optional**: alters may or may not know one another.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
ego_plot(base_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::
:::


---

## The Two Subgraphs of an Ego Network

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- The **star subgraph** contains all the ego-to-alter ties ($E_{ea}$).

. . .

- The **alter-alter subgraph** is the local network among the people who are connected to ego.

. . .

- Alter set: $V = \{a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h\}$

. . .

- Alter-alter ties: $E = \{ab, ah, ag, bh, bg, de, dg, ef, fg, gh\}$

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
ego_plot(base_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::
:::

---

## Ego Network Data: What You Need

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

There are four pieces of information we need to compute the basic ego-network properties:

. . .

1. The **number of ego-alter ties** — the same as the number of alters!

. . .

2. The **number of alter-alter ties**.

. . .

3. **Sociodemographic characteristics of ego**: age, gender, racial identity, class, education.

. . .

4. **Sociodemographic characteristics of alters**: the same attributes, for each alter.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
ego_plot(base_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::
:::

---

## Ego Network Properties: The Menu

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
menu <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Size", "Effective size", "Composition", "Homophily", "Diversity", "Clustering"),
  `Ego-alter ties` = c("✓", "✓", "", "✓", "", ""),
  `Alter-alter ties` = c("", "✓", "", "", "", "✓"),
  `Attributes` = c("", "", "✓", "✓", "✓", ""),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(menu, format = "html", align = "lccc") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 26, bootstrap_options = "condensed", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "16em") |>
  column_spec(2:4, width = "12em")
```

. . .

- Every metric is a different way of summarizing the same small pile of information.

---

## Size

<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Tells us whether your ego network is **large or small** — the number of **alters** (equivalently, ego-alter ties).

</div>

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 33%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
ego_plot(mk_pairs(), alters = c("b", "f"))
```

**Small: Size = 2**
:::

::: {.column style="width: 33%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
ego_plot(mk_pairs(), alters = letters[1:5])
```

**Medium: Size = 5**
:::

::: {.column style="width: 33%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
ego_plot(mk_pairs(), alters = alt_names)
```

**Large: Size = 8**
:::
:::

---

## Effective Size: The Idea

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Still tells us whether your ego network is **large or small**.

. . .

- But **discounts alters who are connected to one another** as redundant.

. . .

- Given by ego-network size minus the **average degree of the alter-alter subgraph**:

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
ego_plot(dense_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::
:::

$$ES = S - \frac{2m}{n}$$

---

## Effective Size: A Dense Alter-Alter Network

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 45%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
ego_plot(dense_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::

::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(adj_kable(dense_pairs, highlight_m = TRUE))
```

- $n = 8$ alters; $m = 14$ ties. Each tie appears twice in the matrix (above and below the diagonal); the shaded 1s count each tie once: $m = 28/2 = 14$.
:::
:::

$$ES = 8 - \frac{28}{8} = 8 - 3.5 = 4.5$$

---

## Effective Size: A Sparse Alter-Alter Network

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 45%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
ego_plot(sparse_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::

::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(adj_kable(sparse_pairs, highlight_m = TRUE))
```

- The shaded 1s give $m = 14/2 = 7$. Same size ($S = 8$), but less redundancy: the sparse network has the **larger effective size**.
:::
:::

$$ES = 8 - \frac{14}{8} = 8 - 1.75 = 6.25$$

---

## Effective Size: The Maximum

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 45%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
ego_plot(kin_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::

::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(adj_kable(kin_pairs))
```

- **No alter-alter ties at all** ($m = 0$): a pure star. No alter is redundant, so nothing gets discounted.
:::
:::

$$ES = 8 - \frac{0}{8} = 8 = S$$

---

## Effective Size: The Minimum

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 45%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
ego_plot(complete_pairs, alters = alt_names)
```
:::

::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(adj_kable(complete_pairs))
```

- **Every alter knows every other** ($m = 28 = \binom{8}{2}$): all alters are mutually redundant, so the whole circle acts like a single effective contact.
:::
:::

$$ES = 8 - \frac{56}{8} = 8 - 7 = 1$$

---

## Composition

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Tells us whether your ego network is **dominated by one category of alters**.

. . .

- Given by the **proportion of alters** who belong to a category: kin, friends, neighbors, co-workers; gender, race, education.

. . .

$$Prop(Kin) = \frac{\text{number of kin alters}}{S}$$

. . .

- Here: $Prop(Kin) = 5/8 = 0.63$ — a **kin-heavy** ego network.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(kin_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = kin_labels,
         pal = c(Kin = "darkorange", "Non-kin" = "steelblue"),
         node_legend = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Composition: Another Example

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Composition can be computed for **any category** the alters fall into.

. . .

- The same network by **gender identity**:

  - $Prop(Men) = 5/8 = 0.63$
  - $Prop(Women) = 2/8 = 0.25$
  - $Prop(Nonbinary) = 1/8 \approx 0.13$

. . .

- Same take: the network is **predominantly male**.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(kin_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = gender_labels,
         pal = gender_pal,
         node_legend = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Homophily: The E-I Index

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Tells us whether the people in your ego network are the **same or different from you** on some sociodemographic characteristic: age, race, gender, education.

. . .

- Example: ego identifies as **Black**. Alters shaded the **same color as ego** share ego's identity ("internal"); all others are "external."

. . .

- $E$ = number of **"External"** alters (different from you); $I$ = number of **"Internal"** alters (same as you).

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
ego_plot(same_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

$$EI = \frac{E - I}{E + I}$$

---

## Homophily: Worked Example and Interpretation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Here: $E = 6$, $I = 2$ (alters **b** and **f** are Black, like ego).

$$EI = \frac{6 - 2}{6 + 2} = \frac{4}{8} = +0.5$$

. . .

- **Negative EI**: preference for "internal" ties. An EI of $-1.0$ is maximum homophily.

. . .

- **Positive EI**: preference for "external" ties. An EI of $+1.0$ is maximum heterophily.

. . .

- **EI = 0**: no preference — equal numbers of internal and external ties. Here, ego's ties lean **external**.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(same_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Homophily: A Homophilous Example

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Flip the pattern: ego (Black) now has **6 Black** alters and **2 White** alters (c and g).

$$EI = \frac{2 - 6}{2 + 6} = \frac{-4}{8} = -0.5$$

. . .

- Same magnitude as before, but on the **homophily** side: ego's ties lean **internal**.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(same_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels_h, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Diversity: Blau's Index

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Tells us whether you tend to connect with a **wide range of others** on some sociodemographic characteristic.

. . .

- Given by **Blau's index of heterogeneity** ($H$):

$$H = 1 - \sum_{k} p_k^2$$

. . .

- **Steps**:

  1. Compute the proportion $p_k$ of alters in each group $k$.
  2. Square each proportion and sum them.
  3. Subtract from 1.0.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(diverse_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE, legend_nrow = 2)
```
:::
:::

---

## Diversity: Worked Example

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Eight alters: 3 White, 2 Black, 2 Asian, 1 Hispanic.

. . .

- **Step 1**, proportions of alters in each group: $p_{\text{W}} = \tfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$, $p_{\text{B}} = \tfrac{2}{8} = 0.250$, $p_{\text{A}} = \tfrac{2}{8} = 0.250$, $p_{\text{H}} = \tfrac{1}{8} = 0.125$.

. . .

- **Steps 2–3**, square each proportion, sum, and subtract from 1.0:

<div class="math-dense" style="font-size: 100%;">

$$H = 1 - \left(0.375^2 + 0.250^2 + 0.250^2 + 0.125^2\right)$$

$$= 1 - 0.281 = 0.72$$

</div>

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(diverse_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE, legend_nrow = 2)
```
:::
:::

---

## Diversity: Interpreting $H$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- A completely homogeneous ego network has $H = 0$ — no diversity among alters.

. . .

- The more diverse the ego network, the closer $H$ is to 1.0.

. . .

- $H$ is at a maximum ($H_{max} = 1 - 1/k$) when alters are spread evenly across $k$ groups. With $k = 4$: $H_{max} = 0.75$, so $H/H_{max} = 0.96$.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(diverse_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE, legend_nrow = 2)
```
:::
:::

---

## Diversity: A Low-Diversity Example

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Reverse the pattern: ego (Black) now has **7 White** alters and **1 Black** alter (f). Only $k = 2$ groups are present.

. . .

- **Step 1**: $p_{\text{W}} = \tfrac{7}{8} = 0.875$, $p_{\text{B}} = \tfrac{1}{8} = 0.125$.

- **Steps 2–3**:

<div class="math-dense" style="font-size: 100%;">

$$H = 1 - \left(0.875^2 + 0.125^2\right) = 1 - 0.781 = 0.22$$

</div>

. . .

- Far below the $H = 0.72$ of the diverse network. With $k = 2$: $H_{max} = 0.5$, so $H/H_{max} = 0.44$ — alters crowd into one group.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(same_pairs, alters = alt_names,
         labels = race_labels_l, pal = race_pal,
         ego_label = "Black",
         node_legend = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Clustering

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Tells us the extent to which your alters are **interconnected among themselves** (know one another) versus **strangers to one another**.

. . .

- Given by the **clustering coefficient** ($CC_i$). You need:

  - The number of **alter-alter ties** ($m$)
  - The number of **alters** ($n$)

. . .

- Don't care about the ego-alter links!

$$CC_i = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}$$

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(clustered_pairs, alters = alt_names, show_ego_ties = FALSE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Clustering: A Clustered Example

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- $n = 8$ alters; $m = 17$ alter-alter ties.

$$CC_i = \frac{2 \times 17}{8 \times 7} = \frac{34}{56} = 0.61$$

. . .

- The ties are **concentrated**: two dense friend circles — everyone knows everyone within their circle — plus a handful of cross-circle ties.

. . .

- The clustering coefficient is the **density of the network formed among your alters** — the probability that two randomly chosen people you know also know one another.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(clustered_pairs, alters = alt_names, show_ego_ties = FALSE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Clustering: A Less Clustered Example

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 42%;"}
<div style="font-size: 90%;">

- Same number of alters ($n = 8$), but only $m = 7$ alter-alter ties.

$$CC_i = \frac{2 \times 7}{8 \times 7} = \frac{14}{56} = 0.25$$

. . .

- The ties are **thinner**: two tight triangles of mutual friends, joined by a single bridge.

. . .

- Same-size ego networks can differ sharply in how **concentrated** their alter-alter ties are — and the clustering coefficient picks this up.

</div>
:::

::: {.column style="width: 58%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
ego_plot(mid_pairs, alters = alt_names, show_ego_ties = FALSE)
```
:::
:::

---

## Clustering: The Extremes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 50%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.8
ego_plot(mk_pairs(), alters = alt_names, show_ego_ties = FALSE)
```

**CC = 0.0** ($m = 0$): none of your friends know one another.
:::

::: {.column style="width: 50%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.8
ego_plot(mk_pairs(t(combn(alt_names, 2))),
         alters = alt_names, show_ego_ties = FALSE)
```

**CC = 1.0** ($m = 28$): every one of your friends knows one another.
:::
:::

---

## Summary: Measuring Ego Networks

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
summ <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Size", "Effective size", "Composition", "Homophily (E-I)", "Diversity (H)", "Clustering (CC)"),
  Question = c(
    "How many alters are in the network?",
    "How large is it net of redundant alters?",
    "Is it dominated by one category of alters?",
    "How similar are alters to ego?",
    "How varied are the attributes of the alters?",
    "To what extent do alters know one another?"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(summ, format = "html", col.names = c("Measure", "Question")) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 20, bootstrap_options = "condensed") |>
  column_spec(1, width = "14em", bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(2, width = "34em")
```

. . .

- Choosing the right metric depends entirely on your research question.
- Homogeneity and diversity are distinct: an ego network can be high on one and low on the other, depending on how the groups are defined.
- Ego clustering measures network density, showing whether an ego is embedded in a single tight-knit circle or bridges separate, unconstrained social worlds.
